newsitem.title: USA: Spain's Telefonica to join Concert - sources.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Telefonica to join Concert - sources.

text.p: Nick Louth
Telefonica de Espana on Friday is to announce it will join the Concert alliance of merger partners British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp., sources close to the deal have said.

They said that British Telecom will take a minority stake in Telefonica and added the Spanish company is expected eventually to leave its Unisource alliance with AT&T Corp. and three other European telecom companies.
"The announcement will be made on Friday from Madrid," one of the sources said late Thursday, declining to be identified.

The resulting alliance brings together Britain's largest phone company, the second largest long distance phone company in the United States and Spain's largest telephone company which also has extensive Latin American interests.
"This is symbolic of the potential of the MCI and BT alliance to steamroller across Europe and the world," said Jeffrey Kagan, who runs his own industry consultantcy.
Neither British Telecom nor Washington-based MCI would comment. It was not immediately possible to contact Telefonica.

The sources said it is not certain whether or not Telefonica will separately take a stake in Concert, which was the name chosen by British Telecom and MCI for their new company when they announced their $20 billion merger in November.

The news was widely expected. The alliance earlier this week signed up Portugal Telecom to join Concert and the Portuguese company let slip in its own announcement a reference to Telefonica joining up with MCI.
For Telefonica it means joining the big league of telecommunications groups, and the British Telecom stake means it will be more tightly bound to its partners than with Unisource.

It will get access to the 40 million Spanish speakers in the United States and in return offers a ticket into Latin America where its Telefonica Internacional unit had sales last year of $2.4 billion.
"Latin America is a huge and growing market, especially in its potential for data services," said Daniel Briere, a consultant at Telechoice.

MCI and British Telecom will be able to leave the Spanish market to its new partner and cut down the number of markets it is pushing into simultaneously with the 1998 liberalisation of European telecommunications.
"France and Germany are obviously more of a priority," said Barry Sine, an analyst at SBC Warburg.

British Telecom is also thought to be pushing hard to get Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp., the Japanese company which is also the world's largest phone company, to be the Asian leg of the alliance.

For AT&T, struggling in a highly competitive market at home, this undermines its efforts to build a powerful international alliance to bring in business from multinational firms and to enter new markets in Europe and Latin America.
"It continues to call into question AT&T's global strategy," said Briere.
AT&T is on Monday expected to report lower first quarter 1997 profits, resulting from its attempts to invest to stay abreast of gathering competitive in the $160 billion U.S. phone marketplace.
Telefonica, Dutch firm Koninklijke PTT Nederland NV, Sweden's Telia and Swiss Telecom each own a 25 percent stake in Unisource, which is affiliated to AT&T.
Concert is also competing with Global One, an alliance of Germany's Deutsche Telekom AG, France Telecom and the third largest U.S. long distance telephone carrier, Sprint Corp.
